hero.title: Find the right enclosure for the way you actually deploy
hero.subtitle: Five questions on site, capacity, power, cooling, and access. We rank the enclosure families that fit and show you live inventory.
hero.body: Built for network and facilities teams specifying racks for edge sites, IDF rooms, and data center halls.

questions.title: Where will this rack live?
questions.description: Site conditions drive depth, mounting, and how much you can rely on ambient air.
questions.supportCopy: Pick the environment closest to your install.

answers.label: Branch or retail closet
answers.subtitle: Shared space, no raised floor
answers.description: Often a wall or a corner of a utility room.

answers.label: Office IDF room
answers.subtitle: Dedicated but shared with building services
answers.description: A floor-level distribution room serving one or two floors.

answers.label: Dedicated server room
answers.subtitle: Conditioned, access-controlled
answers.description: A room built for equipment, with its own cooling.

answers.label: Data center hall
answers.subtitle: Row-and-aisle layout
answers.description: Structured power, containment, and row-level cooling.

questions.title: How much equipment are you mounting?
questions.description: Usable rack units, counting the growth you already know about.
questions.supportCopy: Estimate high — headroom is cheaper than a second rack.

answers.label: Under 12U
answers.subtitle: A switch, a patch panel, a small UPS
answers.description: Fits a wall-mount enclosure.

answers.label: 12U to 24U
answers.subtitle: A stack plus storage
answers.description: Outgrowing wall-mount; needs a floor enclosure.

answers.label: 25U to 42U
answers.subtitle: A full closet or small room
answers.description: Standard full-height territory.

answers.label: 42U or multiple racks
answers.subtitle: Row-scale deployment
answers.description: Buying in rows, not units.

questions.title: What is the power draw per rack?
questions.description: Steady-state load, not nameplate. This is the single strongest signal for cooling.
questions.supportCopy: If you are unsure, use your PDU's reported load.

answers.label: Under 2kW
answers.subtitle: Switching and light compute
answers.description: Ambient air is fine.

answers.label: 2kW to 5kW
answers.subtitle: Mixed switching and servers
answers.description: Standard airflow handles this.

answers.label: 5kW to 10kW
answers.subtitle: Dense compute
answers.description: Needs deliberate airflow planning.

answers.label: Over 10kW
answers.subtitle: High-density compute or GPU
answers.description: Ambient air will not carry this.

questions.title: How is heat handled today?
questions.description: Your existing cooling approach constrains which enclosures are viable.
questions.supportCopy: Choose what is actually installed, not what is planned.

answers.label: Ambient room air
answers.subtitle: No dedicated cooling
answers.description: Building HVAC only.

answers.label: Passive front-to-back airflow
answers.subtitle: Perforated doors, blanking panels
answers.description: Directed airflow, no active cooling in the rack.

answers.label: In-row or rack-mount cooling
answers.subtitle: Active cooling at the rack
answers.description: Cooling sits in the row with the load.

answers.label: Contained hot or cold aisle
answers.subtitle: Full containment
answers.description: Aisle-level containment with row cooling.

questions.title: What access control do you need?
questions.description: Shared and unattended spaces usually need more than a latch.
questions.supportCopy: Compliance requirements often decide this one.

answers.label: Open frame
answers.subtitle: No doors
answers.description: Maximum access and airflow, no physical security.

answers.label: Locking doors
answers.subtitle: Keyed front and rear
answers.description: Standard for shared rooms.

answers.label: Keyed with audit trail
answers.subtitle: Logged access
answers.description: Tracks who opened the rack and when.

answers.label: Biometric or badge
answers.subtitle: Credentialed entry
answers.description: Integrated with facility access control.

personas.title: Edge Site Builder
personas.description: You are standing up networking in branch offices, retail sites, or closets where floor space is scarce and nobody is on site to service it.

collection.title: Wall-Mount & Low-U Enclosures
collection.description: Shallow, lockable enclosures that mount to a wall and hold a switch, a patch panel, and a small UPS.

personas.title: Growing Network
personas.description: Your switch count keeps climbing and the closet you inherited is out of room, out of ports, and out of airflow.

collection.title: Mid-Height Network Enclosures
collection.description: 24U to 42U enclosures with the cable management and airflow to keep a growing switch stack serviceable.

personas.title: Core Data Center
personas.description: You run a dedicated room or hall and buy racks by the row, with structured power and cooling already in the plan.

collection.title: Full-Height Server Racks
collection.description: 42U and taller open-frame and enclosed racks built for structured deployment at row scale.

personas.title: High-Density Compute
personas.description: Your per-rack power draw is well past what ambient air can carry, so cooling and power distribution drive the rack choice.

collection.title: Cooling & Critical Power
collection.description: In-row cooling and rack-mount UPS sized for high-draw compute where thermal headroom is the constraint.

crossCategoryModules.title: Switching
crossCategoryModules.description: Access and aggregation switches sized for the port count you just described.

crossCategoryModules.title: Cables & Management
crossCategoryModules.description: Patch cable and management hardware — the difference between a rack you can service and one you cannot.

crossCategoryModules.title: Critical Power
crossCategoryModules.description: Rack-mount UPS and power distribution matched to the draw you reported.
